But p_12 (x) was defined earlier as: "Everyone who either keeps a journal or writes short stories (but not both) practices writing."

So p_12 (x): (p_1 (x) ⊕ p_2 (x)) → p_12 (x), means "if x does exactly one of journal or short stories, then x practices writing".

But ¬p_12 (Quincy) means "Quincy does NOT practice writing", which is not logically equivalent to the consequent of that implication.

The predicate p_12 (Quincy) being false does not necessarily mean "Quincy does not practice writing" — it could mean the condition (p_1 ⊕ p_2) is false, or that even if it’s true, he doesn’t practice writing. In fact, p_12 (x)

might mean "x practices writing" under that condition, but it is not the definition of "practices writing" itself.

So interpreting ¬p_12 (Quincy)
as "Quincy does not practice writing" incorrectly treats p_12 as equivalent to "practices writing", ignoring the conditional context in which it was introduced.

So the FOL to NL mapping assumes p_12 (x)
is "x practices writing", but actually p_12 (x)
is a placeholder that is asserted true when the antecedent holds — so equating it directly to "practices writing" is only valid under that condition. Thus, the atomic negation ¬p_12 (Quincy)
cannot be directly read as "does not practice writing" without knowing whether the antecedent holds.

Therefore, it’s a misinterpretation to treat p_12 (x)
as synonymous with "practices writing" in all contexts. The NL treats it as a direct predicate, but the FOL defines it as a consequent, not a definition.
